## Research Question, Literature Review, and Some Terminology

When initially determining how to calculate optimal outfielder position, a clear research question emerged:

```         
Given a specific batter is in the box, what are the optimal positions for an opposing team’s outfielders? 
```

This, of course, eventually gave away to the 'how' of the question, which lead me to a few papers published and presentations given within the past five years. Each have different methods of determining an outfield's position. In chronological order, these are the ones I utilized the most (and this list is not exhaustive by any means):

- Anthony Montes' paper “Optimizing Outfield Positioning: Creating an Area-Based Alignment Using Outfielder Ability and Hitter Tendencies” [[Link]](https://sabr.org/journal/article/optimizing-outfield-positioning-creating-an-area-based-alignment-using-outfielder-ability-and-hitter-tendencies/) describes a methodology of creating a covering of batted ball data with three outfielders. Topologically, a covering of a space can be intuited as a map where the every point in the space can be mapped onto the cover (there are other properties, but I am not a topologist. I got a C in that class in college.). A best-covering, in this application, is a cover compromised of three circles that encompasses the most batted balls, the radii of which represent a fielder's catch radius. The fastest fielder, typically the center-fielder, is placed first to cover the most balls. Then, the next-fastest fielder is placed to cover the most remaining batted balls, then the third fielder is placed the same. This covering sometimes eschews traditional outfielder placement by vertically stacking or clustering outfielders together. The actual calculations are done within an R program called Outfielder Player Positioning Optimizer (OPPO), but the source code is unavailable.

- Dr. Elizabeth Bouzarth's paper "Swing Shift: A Mathematical Approach to Defensive Positioning in Baseball" [[Link]](https://www.sloansportsconference.com/research-papers/swing-shift-a-mathematical-approach-to-defensive-positioning-in-baseball) looks at positioning for all fielders in two categories: three-infielder sets and four-infielder sets. The field is partitioned into an infield and outfield, and then a set of 5-foot discs where fielders can be positioned. Fielders are placed in each disc against the batted balls of certain batters and given a 'coverage score' based on their ability to field a given ball. These coverage scores account for fielders having less time field a ball they need to move forward for, creating more realistic zones in which a fielder can react. Fielders are then positioned such that their coverage scores are maximized, which aims to minimize batting average on balls in play (BABIP).

- Dr. Alan Murray's paper "Enhancing strategic defensive positioning and performance in the outfield" [[Link]](http://doi.org/10.1007/s10109-021-00367-1) uses a linear programming / spatial optimization model to attempt to optimize outfielder positioning at the collegiate level. The model attempts to maximize fielders being present in high-value locations of batted balls $a_i$ (locations being set $I$) while minimizing distances $d_{ij}$ (potential fielder positions being set $J$), and optimizing using the framework across certain batters returns optimal fielder positions. The optimal positions that emerge differ for certain batters depending on which objective is prioritized within the model, and it does not treat all batted balls as equal. The exact function for value is not given, but it is a random forest model with a range of 1 to 5.09 with exit velocity, launch angle, and MLB run value of batted ball type as inputs.

- Dr. William Melville's paper "Optimizing Baseball Fielder Positioning with Consideration for Adaptable Hitters" [[Link]](https://www.sloansportsconference.com/research-papers/optimizing-baseball-fielder-positioning-with-consideration-for-adaptable-hitters) analyzes the infield shift (which was banned in 2023, but the paper notes this) but addresses outfielder positioning as well. A machine learning algorithm is used to calculate $f_{woba}$, the effective weighted on-base average of a batted ball that is not caught, and $f$, the probability that a given batted ball is fielded for an out. This model is able to account for hitters that are adept at finding gaps in defensive positioning via calculating a positioning strategy $p_s$ based on a set of possible actions a batter can take in the box $\mathcal{D}$. The two examples the paper uses are $\mathcal{D} = {\text\{bunt,swing\}}$ and $\mathcal{D} = {\text\{pull,oppo\}}$ -- i.e., hitters can choose to swing or tactically bunt, or hitters can choose halves of the field to hit the ball to.

From my literature review, I knew that I wanted to differentiate my work by considering the batted balls as dynamic objects instead of a set of points within the outfield. I'm also quite familiar with the physics of baseballs in flight from my work on my senior thesis, *[The Modern Baseball Pitch: A Physical Perspective](https://bit.ly/mbp-pp-cc)*. Batted balls have a calculable hang time which is determined by the initial conditions with which they leave the bat. Ignoring the aerial space effects such as wind, temperature, and air density, these initial conditions are the angle the ball is hit relative to the plane of the field ([launch angle](https://www.mlb.com/glossary/statcast/launch-angle) $\theta$) and the speed with which it leaves the bat ([exit velocity](https://www.mlb.com/glossary/statcast/exit-velocity) $v$). With a constant acceleration due to gravity $g$, hang time is determined by $t = 2v \sin{\theta} / g$.

This time is used to calculate a ball's ***competitive area*** (or ***catchable radius***), which is based on an outfielder's speed and reaction time. Speed is measured via a player's [sprint speed](https://www.mlb.com/glossary/statcast/sprint-speed) $s$, which is calculated with a mix of one-second top speeds from home to first base and most runs of two bases or more. Reaction time is a bit trickier to measure, but is depicted via Baseball Savant's [Outfielder Jump leaderboard](https://baseballsavant.mlb.com/leaderboard/outfield_jump) $j$ in the form of three statistics: 'Reaction', 'Burst', and 'Route'. Reaction and Burst depict the distance in feet traveled in any direction within the first 1.5 seconds and next 1.5 seconds of an outfield play, respectively, while Route represents the distance in feet covered against the direct route within the same three-second window. These three statistics additively combine into ***outfielder jump***. Each of these three numbers are measured relative to league average, meaning that a remarkably fast player that is bad at reading a direct route to balls can still have a negative jump. With all of this, a circle around a given batted ball location with a radius of $(t-.4)*s+j$ can be constructed as a batted ball's competitive area.

## Massaging StatCast Data

Baseball Savant is the host of MLB's Statcast, a database containing tracking data from Trackman cameras installed in ballparks ahead of the 2015 season. In short, it has revolutionized the game and produces a bevy of useful data but not in a state that we can accurately utilize without some transformation.

Statcast has batted ball location data for every ball in play, but it only represents *where* a fielder picks up a ball with coordinates $(h_x,h_y)$ instead of where it lands. I will call the former of these locations the ***Statcast batted ball location*** and the latter the ***true batted ball location***. An example of this can be seen with [this batted ball from Pete Crow-Armstrong](https://baseballsavant.mlb.com/sporty-videos?playId=0dfc3fb4-ac31-314e-983a-349ac5d62394) that takes a sharp hop over the pitcher's mound just past the infield dirt. Statcast places this ball where Cooper Pratt fields it instead of where it originally hit the ground. Statcast's coordinate system also places home plate at $(x,y)$ coordinates of (125.42, -198.27) and bases batted ball data off of this point, which is inconvenient for our purposes. Thus, we create a new coordinate system $(x',y')$ that is a direct translation of the existing coordinate system such that home plate is (0,0).

Since we are only considering balls in the outfield, a good approximation of where a ball actually lands can be calculated via the ***spray angle*** of the ball $\phi$. $\phi$ in this case is the angle relative to the back of home plate that the ball travels, with the foul lines being represented by $-\frac{\pi}{4}$ and $\frac{\pi}{4}$. This is not something natively measured by Statcast but it can be calculated via taking the Statcast batted ball location and finding the angle between it and the back of home plate via $$\arctan(\frac{hc_x - 125.42}{198.27 - hc_y})$$ (Albert 2025). Statcast measures the exit velocity and launch angle of batted balls to find a projected distance $d$, and using this information alongside spray angle can give us the true batted ball location $(t_x,t_y)$ via $$t_x = d\sin{\phi}, t_y = d\cos{\phi}.$$ These true batted ball locations are what is utilized throughout the package and all of these operations occur within `getBattedBallData()`.

## Optimal Position Algorithm

Once a batter and fielder is determined and the batted ball dataset is constructed, the ***optimal position*** would be determined by where the outfielder could start that allows them to catch the most balls within their part of the field (left, center, right, as determined in the below section). Extra base hits are not considered with any additional value, as the goal is to maximize put-outs. This is done by splitting the field into points 3 inches apart and storing the list of points within each batted ball's competitive area in the function `getCompetitiveArea()`. Then, for all batted balls, the ($t_x$,$t_y$) coordinate pairs are grouped by count which causes a maximum number of instances to occur -- the region of points that shows up that amount of times is called the ***optimal hull***, called as such because it is inherently convex.

In graph theory, this is called the *maximum clique* of the graph of the field as split into points. I personally find it a bit easier to intuit in the language of set theory, where if the batted ball competitive areas $B_c$ form a set $\mathcal{B}_c$, we are looking for the intersection of the cartesian product of all $B_c$ with the greatest cardinality. In non-math terms, it's the area where the most circles overlap.

Once the optimal hull is determined, the centroid of the region is said to be the optimal position (or ***optimal point***) where an outfielder should start versus the batter. Any hull that is more than one point allows variance in positioning for an outfielder that will let them catch any ball whose competitive area intersects it.

## Constants, Constraints, and Assumptions

- A ball is considered caught by an outfielder if they are able to arrive to the true batted ball location from their starting position .4 seconds or sooner before the ball hits the ground. This .4 was chosen based on a short film study of difficult outfield catches, and I intuitively believe that this is a reasonable amount of time for an outfielder to coordinate sticking out their glove for a catch.

- `getCompetitiveArea()` was chosen to allow 16 positions per square foot, or have a 3-inch resolution, to balance computational run time with precision of positioning. In an actual game situation within an expansive outfield, players situate themselves within a certain part of the outfield relative to landmarks of the outfield wall or design around them as opposed to an inch-accurate set of coordinates. An article displaying the Royals' outfield strategy in 2018 confirms this, showing outfielders receive directions as opposed to coordinates (Judge 2018). This makes it reasonable to sacrifice some resolution in positioning, since the algorithm takes quadratic time.

- 127 feet, as measured by Statcast, is chosen as the minimum distance for a batted ball to be considered. This ensures that balls get past the infield, which is measured as a 95-foot radius from the front-center of the pitching rubber. Our coordinate system being centered at home plate and infield being centered around the pitcher's mound makes it awkward to create a clean filter, and 127 feet is the minimum distance between the edge of the infield and home plate.

- $\pm\frac{\phi}{9}$, or $\pm20^\circ$, is arbitrarily used as the cutoff for center field as it splits the outfield defined by $\pm\frac{\phi}{4}$ into three regions. With this split, center field covers 40 degrees of the 90 degrees of viable outfield while the other outfielders cover the remaining 25 degrees on each side. In actuality, corner outfielders are also covering foul territory which is not considered in the positioning algorithm, and the regions each outfielder cover are more equal than a 25/25/40 degree split.

- Park walls are approximated using [Andrew Clem's stadium maps](http://www.andrewclem.com/Baseball/Stadium_lists.html), a massively useful resource depicting hand-drawn pixel diagrams of every MLB stadium. Using home plate as the origin and scaling these diagrams to known left- and right-field dimensions allowed me to construct a path of each stadium's outfield. I arbitrarily chose 2020 as the cutoff, as these paths were manually pulled from the diagrams. Paths are stored a set of points in order to play nicely with polygon-based functions in R -- as a result, curves within outfield walls are approximated by sets of points instead of a function.

- Besides assumptions made earlier, optimal position also does not consider game situations that necessitate different positioning, the pitcher on the mound, or outfielder arm strength. It is purely a measure to maximize put-outs against a batter's given spray chart within the outfield.
